chapterTitle: The Revelation of Jesus Christ and the Son of Man Among the Lampstands
themeTitle: “I Am the First and the Last, and the Living One”

scripture.text: This is the Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show to his servants the things which must happen soon, which he sent and made known by his angel to his servant, John,
scripture.understanding: Ἀποκάλυψις Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, “This is the Revelation of Jesus Christ” — ἀποκάλυψις, from the appear family: an unveiling, the drawing back of a curtain. It is both from Jesus and about Jesus. ἣν ἔδωκεν αὐτῷ ὁ θεὸς δεῖξαι τοῖς δούλοις αὐτοῦ, “which God gave him to show to his servants” — δοῦλος, from the servant family: a bondservant, owned by and devoted to a master. ἃ δεῖ γενέσθαι ἐν τάχει, “the things which must happen soon” — δεῖ, it is necessary: God's plan will certainly be done. καὶ ἐσήμανεν, “and made known” — σημαίνω, to signify, to show by signs: the book will speak in pictures.

scripture.text: who testified to God’s word, and of the testimony of Jesus Christ, about everything that he saw.
scripture.understanding: ὃς ἐμαρτύρησεν τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ, “who testified to God’s word” — μαρτυρέω, from the witness family; λόγος, from the word family. καὶ τὴν μαρτυρίαν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, “and of the testimony of Jesus Christ” — μαρτυρία, also from the witness family: the testimony Jesus gave, and the testimony about Him. Two members of one family in one verse: John testifies to the testimony. ὅσα εἶδεν, “about everything that he saw” — εἴδω, from the see family (and the know family): this book is an eyewitness report of a vision.

scripture.text: Blessed is he who reads and those who hear the words of the prophecy, and keep the things that are written in it, for the time is at hand.
scripture.understanding: μακάριος ὁ ἀναγινώσκων καὶ οἱ ἀκούοντες, “Blessed is he who reads and those who hear the words of the prophecy” — λόγος, from the word family. This is the first of seven blessings in Revelation (1:3; 14:13; 16:15; 19:9; 20:6; 22:7, 14). One person reads aloud in the church; the congregation listens. καὶ τηροῦντες τὰ ἐν αὐτῇ γεγραμμένα, “and keep the things that are written in it” — τηρέω, from the hold family: to guard and obey. The blessing is not for decoding but for keeping. ὁ γὰρ καιρὸς ἐγγύς, “for the time is at hand” — καιρός, from the time family: the decisive season, not mere χρόνος, clock-time.

scripture.text: John, to the seven assemblies that are in Asia: Grace to you and peace, from God, who is and who was and who is to come; and from the seven Spirits who are before his throne;
scripture.understanding: Ἰωάννης ταῖς ἑπτὰ ἐκκλησίαις ταῖς ἐν τῇ Ἀσίᾳ, “John, to the seven assemblies that are in Asia” — the Roman province of Asia, in modern western Turkey. Seven is the number of completeness: these seven real churches also stand for the whole church. χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη, “Grace to you and peace” — Paul's greeting. ἀπὸ ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος, “from God, who is and who was and who is to come” — echoing God's name revealed to Moses, ‘I AM’. καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν ἑπτὰ πνευμάτων, “and from the seven Spirits who are before his throne” — the strongest reading is the Holy Spirit in His fullness (Zechariah 4:2–10 speaks of seven lamps as the eyes of the Lord); others think of seven angels. θρόνος, throne, appears over forty times in this book.

scripture.text: and from Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth. To him who loves us, and washed us from our sins by his blood;
scripture.understanding: καὶ ἀπὸ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, ὁ μάρτυς ὁ πιστός, “and from Jesus Christ, the faithful witness” — μάρτυς, from the witness family: the one who testifies; by the end of the first century the word was coming to mean one who dies for the testimony. ὁ πρωτότοκος τῶν νεκρῶν, “the firstborn of the dead” — first to rise to unending life, and heir. καὶ ὁ ἄρχων τῶν βασιλέων τῆς γῆς, “and the ruler of the kings of the earth” — γῆ, from the world family. Three titles: faithful in death, risen from death, reigning over all. Τῷ ἀγαπῶντι ἡμᾶς, “To him who loves us” — ἀγαπάω, from the love family, present tense: He keeps on loving us. καὶ λούσαντι ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν ἐν τῷ αἵματι αὐτοῦ, “and washed us from our sins by his blood” — ἁμαρτία, from the sin family. The WEB follows manuscripts reading λούσαντι, ‘washed’; the oldest read λύσαντι, ‘freed’ or ‘loosed’ — one letter's difference; both are true.

scripture.text: and he made us to be a Kingdom, priests to his God and Father; to him be the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.
scripture.understanding: καὶ ἐποίησεν ἡμᾶς βασιλείαν, ἱερεῖς τῷ θεῷ καὶ πατρὶ αὐτοῦ, “and he made us to be a Kingdom, priests to his God and Father” — God's words to Israel at Sinai, ‘a kingdom of priests’, are now fulfilled in the church: every believer has access to God and represents Him to the world. αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων, “to him be the glory and the dominion forever and ever” — κράτος, from the power family: ruling might, power that prevails, as distinct from δύναμις, ability; αἰών, from the time family and the world family, doubled: ‘to the ages of the ages’.

scripture.text: Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, including those who pierced him. All the tribes of the earth will mourn over him. Even so, Amen.
scripture.understanding: Ἰδοὺ ἔρχεται μετὰ τῶν νεφελῶν, “Behold, he is coming with the clouds” — Daniel saw ‘one like a son of man’ coming with the clouds of heaven to receive a kingdom; Jesus applied it to Himself. καὶ ὄψεται αὐτὸν πᾶς ὀφθαλμὸς καὶ οἵτινες αὐτὸν ἐξεκέντησαν, “and every eye will see him, including those who pierced him” — ὁράω, from the see family; and ‘all the tribes of the earth’ — γῆ, from the world family; ἐκκεντέω, to pierce through, from Zechariah: “they will look to me whom they have pierced” (Zechariah 12:10). κόπτω, to beat the breast in mourning: the whole earth will mourn when He appears. ναί, ἀμήν, “Even so, Amen” — Greek and Hebrew ‘yes’ side by side.

scripture.text: “I am the Alpha and the Omega,” says the Lord God, “who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty.”
scripture.understanding: Ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ Ἄλφα καὶ τὸ Ὦ, “I am the Alpha and the Omega” — the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet: God is the beginning and the end of everything, and everything between. λέγει κύριος ὁ θεός, “says the Lord God” — one of only two places in Revelation where God the Father speaks directly (with 21:5–8). ὁ παντοκράτωρ, “the Almighty” — παντοκράτωρ, the all-ruling, from πᾶς and κράτος: used nine times in Revelation and only once elsewhere in the New Testament. Caesar claimed to rule the world; God alone holds all things.

scripture.text: I John, your brother and partner with you in the oppression, Kingdom, and perseverance in Christ Jesus, was on the isle that is called Patmos because of God’s Word and the testimony of Jesus Christ.
scripture.understanding: Ἐγὼ Ἰωάννης, ὁ ἀδελφὸς ὑμῶν καὶ συγκοινωνὸς ἐν τῇ θλίψει καὶ βασιλείᾳ καὶ ὑπομονῇ ἐν Ἰησοῦ, “I John, your brother and partner with you in the oppression, Kingdom, and perseverance in Christ Jesus” — not a superior but a fellow-sufferer. θλῖψις, pressure, crushing affliction; βασιλεία, the reign of God; ὑπομονή, from the endurance family: remaining under the load. All three belong together, held by one Greek article: the kingdom is entered through pressure and endurance. ἐν τῇ νήσῳ τῇ καλουμένῃ Πάτμῳ διὰ τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ, “on the isle that is called Patmos because of God’s Word” — λόγος, from the word family. Patmos was a small rocky island used for banishment. καὶ τὴν μαρτυρίαν Ἰησοῦ, “the testimony of Jesus Christ” — μαρτυρία, from the witness family.

scripture.text: I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day, and I heard behind me a loud voice, like a trumpet
scripture.understanding: ἐγενόμην ἐν πνεύματι, “I was in the Spirit” — caught up by the Holy Spirit into a state of vision, like Ezekiel. ἐν τῇ κυριακῇ ἡμέρᾳ, “on the Lord’s day” — κυριακός, belonging to the Lord; ἡμέρα, from the time family. The strongest reading is Sunday, the day of the resurrection, when Christians met for worship; Caesar had his ‘imperial day’, but the church had the Lord's. καὶ ἤκουσα ὀπίσω μου φωνὴν μεγάλην ὡς σάλπιγγος, “and I heard behind me a loud voice, like a trumpet” — the trumpet sounded at Sinai when God came down.

scripture.text: saying, “What you see, write in a book and send to the seven assemblies: to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and to Laodicea.”
scripture.understanding: λεγούσης· ὃ βλέπεις γράψον εἰς βιβλίον, “saying, ‘What you see, write in a book’” — βλέπω, from the see family: to look at, present tense — keep watching and keep writing. βιβλίον, from the book family: a scroll, as distinct from βίβλος, a volume or record (3:5). καὶ πέμψον ταῖς ἑπτὰ ἐκκλησίαις, “and send to the seven assemblies” — the seven cities lie on a circular road, in the order a messenger would travel: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea.

scripture.text: I turned to see the voice that spoke with me. Having turned, I saw seven golden lamp stands.
scripture.understanding: Καὶ ἐπέστρεψα βλέπειν τὴν φωνὴν ἥτις ἐλάλει μετ᾽ ἐμοῦ, “I turned to see the voice that spoke with me” — βλέπω, from the see family. καὶ ἐπιστρέψας εἶδον ἑπτὰ λυχνίας χρυσᾶς, “Having turned, I saw seven golden lamp stands” — εἴδω, also from the see family (and the know family): βλέπω is the act of looking, εἶδον what he actually saw. λυχνία, a lampstand: in the tabernacle there was one lampstand with seven lamps; Zechariah saw “a lamp stand all of gold, with its bowl on the top of it” (Zechariah 4:2). Now there are seven lampstands — the churches, carrying the light of God into the world (1:20).

scripture.text: And among the lamp stands was one like a son of man, clothed with a robe reaching down to his feet, and with a golden sash around his chest.
scripture.understanding: καὶ ἐν μέσῳ τῶν λυχνιῶν ὅμοιον υἱὸν ἀνθρώπου, “And among the lamp stands was one like a son of man” — Daniel's heavenly figure (‘one like a son of man’), and Jesus' favourite title for Himself. He is not far off; He walks among His churches. ἐνδεδυμένον ποδήρη, “clothed with a robe reaching down to his feet” — ποδήρης, the long robe of a priest. καὶ περιεζωσμένον πρὸς τοῖς μαστοῖς ζώνην χρυσᾶν, “and with a golden sash around his chest” — royal and priestly dress: He is King and High Priest.

scripture.text: His head and his hair were white as white wool, like snow. His eyes were like a flame of fire.
scripture.understanding: ἡ δὲ κεφαλὴ αὐτοῦ καὶ αἱ τρίχες λευκαὶ ὡς ἔριον λευκόν ὡς χιών, “His head and his hair were white as white wool, like snow” — in Daniel's vision the Ancient of Days had hair ‘like pure wool’. What Daniel saw of God, John sees in Jesus: eternity, wisdom and purity. καὶ οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ αὐτοῦ ὡς φλὸξ πυρός, “His eyes were like a flame of fire” — φλόξ, a blaze: eyes that see through every pretence (2:18, 23).

scripture.text: His feet were like burnished brass, as if it had been refined in a furnace. His voice was like the voice of many waters.
scripture.understanding: καὶ οἱ πόδες αὐτοῦ ὅμοιοι χαλκολιβάνῳ ὡς ἐν καμίνῳ πεπυρωμένης, “His feet were like burnished brass, as if it had been refined in a furnace” — χαλκολίβανον, a rare word for a glowing metal alloy; Thyatira, a city of metal-workers' guilds, would hear it (2:18). Feet of strength and stability, refined by fire. καὶ ἡ φωνὴ αὐτοῦ ὡς φωνὴ ὑδάτων πολλῶν, “His voice was like the voice of many waters” — Ezekiel heard God's voice like the sound of many waters; on Patmos the surf crashed on every side.

scripture.text: He had seven stars in his right hand. Out of his mouth proceeded a sharp two-edged sword. His face was like the sun shining at its brightest.
scripture.understanding: καὶ ἔχων ἐν τῇ δεξιᾷ χειρὶ αὐτοῦ ἀστέρας ἑπτά, “He had seven stars in his right hand” — ἀστήρ: Roman coins showed Domitian's dead infant son as a god holding seven stars. The real Lord of the stars is Christ, who holds His churches' messengers in His hand. καὶ ἐκ τοῦ στόματος αὐτοῦ ῥομφαία δίστομος ὀξεῖα ἐκπορευομένη, “Out of his mouth proceeded a sharp two-edged sword” — ῥομφαία, a long sword: His word judges and conquers (2:12, 16; 19:15). καὶ ἡ ὄψις αὐτοῦ ὡς ὁ ἥλιος φαίνει ἐν τῇ δυνάμει αὐτοῦ, “His face was like the sun shining at its brightest” — δύναμις, from the power family: literally ‘in its power’, its full inherent strength; the WEB renders it ‘brightest’. φαίνω, from the appear family: to shine, to give light. This is the face Peter, James and John saw on the mountain.

scripture.text: When I saw him, I fell at his feet like a dead man. He laid his right hand on me, saying, “Don’t be afraid. I am the first and the last,
scripture.understanding: Καὶ ὅτε εἶδον αὐτόν, ἔπεσα πρὸς τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ ὡς νεκρός, “When I saw him, I fell at his feet like a dead man” — εἴδω, from the see family (and the know family). The disciple who once leaned on Jesus' chest now collapses before His glory. καὶ ἔθηκεν τὴν δεξιὰν αὐτοῦ ἐπ᾽ ἐμὲ λέγων· μὴ φοβοῦ, “He laid his right hand on me, saying, ‘Don’t be afraid’” — the same hand that holds the stars touches the trembling disciple. φοβέομαι, to be afraid. ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ὁ ἔσχατος, “I am the first and the last” — God's title in Isaiah (‘I am the first, and I am the last’), now spoken by Jesus.

scripture.text: and the Living one. I was dead, and behold, I am alive forever and ever. Amen. I have the keys of Death and of Hades.
scripture.understanding: καὶ ὁ ζῶν, “and the Living one” — ζάω, from the life family: not merely one who lives, but the source of life. καὶ ἐγενόμην νεκρὸς καὶ ἰδοὺ ζῶν εἰμι εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων, “I was dead, and behold, I am alive forever and ever” — ζάω again; αἰών, from the time family and the world family: the resurrection in one sentence. καὶ ἔχω τὰς κλεῖς τοῦ θανάτου καὶ τοῦ ᾅδου, “I have the keys of Death and of Hades” — κλείς, a key: authority to open and shut. ᾅδης, the realm of the dead. The believer facing a Roman sword need not fear: Jesus holds the keys.

scripture.text: Write therefore the things which you have seen, and the things which are, and the things which will happen hereafter;
scripture.understanding: γράψον οὖν ἃ εἶδες καὶ ἃ εἰσὶν καὶ ἃ μέλλει γενέσθαι μετὰ ταῦτα, “Write therefore the things which you have seen, and the things which are, and the things which will happen hereafter” — εἴδω, from the see family (and the know family); μέλλω, to be about to. Many read this as an outline of the book: the vision just seen (ch. 1), the present state of the churches (chs. 2–3), and what follows (chs. 4–22). Others take it as saying that the whole vision concerns both present and future.

scripture.text: the mystery of the seven stars which you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lamp stands. The seven stars are the angels of the seven assemblies. The seven lamp stands are seven assemblies.
scripture.understanding: τὸ μυστήριον τῶν ἑπτὰ ἀστέρων, “the mystery of the seven stars” — μυστήριον, a secret now revealed. οἱ ἑπτὰ ἀστέρες ἄγγελοι τῶν ἑπτὰ ἐκκλησιῶν εἰσιν, “The seven stars are the angels of the seven assemblies” — ἄγγελος means both ‘angel’ and ‘messenger’. Some think of guardian angels of the churches; others of the churches' leaders or messengers; others of the heavenly side of each church. καὶ αἱ λυχνίαι αἱ ἑπτὰ ἑπτὰ ἐκκλησίαι εἰσίν, “The seven lamp stands are seven assemblies” — the church exists to hold up the light.

visualMeditations.title: The Voice Behind You
visualMeditations.image: Picture an old man on a bare, rocky island, the sea on every side. He is in exile for preaching Jesus. It is Sunday; far away his churches are gathering without him. He bows to pray — and suddenly a voice like a trumpet blasts behind him. He turns around.
visualMeditations.meaning: “I John, your brother and partner with you in the oppression, Kingdom, and perseverance in Christ Jesus, was on the isle that is called Patmos because of God’s Word and the testimony of Jesus Christ” (v. 9). “I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day, and I heard behind me a loud voice, like a trumpet” (v. 10). The loneliest places of faithfulness are often where Jesus reveals Himself most clearly.

visualMeditations.title: The Son of Man Among the Lampstands
visualMeditations.image: Picture seven tall golden lampstands, their flames flickering. Walking among them is a figure in a long robe with a golden sash, hair white as snow, eyes like blazing fire, feet glowing like metal in a furnace, a sword coming from His mouth, His face shining like the noonday sun.
visualMeditations.meaning: “And among the lamp stands was one like a son of man, clothed with a robe reaching down to his feet, and with a golden sash around his chest” (v. 13). Jesus is not absent from His church. He walks among the lampstands, sees everything, tends the flames, and speaks with a word sharper than any sword.

visualMeditations.title: The Right Hand
visualMeditations.image: Picture seven bright stars held in a strong right hand. Then see John collapse on the ground like a corpse — and the same right hand reach down and rest gently on his shoulder.
visualMeditations.meaning: “When I saw him, I fell at his feet like a dead man. He laid his right hand on me, saying, ‘Don’t be afraid. I am the first and the last’” (v. 17). The hand that holds the stars is the hand that holds you. His glory would crush you; His grace lifts you.

visualMeditations.title: The Keys
visualMeditations.image: Picture a great ring of iron keys, the keys to the prison of death and the grave. For all of human history they have hung on the enemy's belt. Now see them in the hand of the risen Jesus, scarred by the nails.
visualMeditations.meaning: “I was dead, and behold, I am alive forever and ever. Amen. I have the keys of Death and of Hades” (v. 18). The worst that any persecutor can do is send a believer through a door whose key Jesus holds. Death is not the end; it is a door He opens.

structure.label: Prologue and Blessing (v. 1-3)
structure.body: The revelation comes from God, through Jesus Christ and His angel, to John and to Christ's servants; a blessing is promised to those who read, hear and keep it, for the time is near.

structure.label: Greeting and Doxology (v. 4-8)
structure.body: John greets the seven churches with grace and peace from the eternal God, the sevenfold Spirit and Jesus Christ the faithful witness; he praises the One who loves us, freed us by His blood and made us a kingdom of priests; Christ is coming with the clouds, and God declares Himself the Alpha and Omega, the Almighty.

structure.label: The Vision of the Son of Man (v. 9-16)
structure.body: On Patmos, on the Lord's day, John hears a trumpet voice telling him to write to the seven churches; he turns and sees seven golden lampstands and among them one like a son of man, robed as priest and king, with white hair, fiery eyes, glowing feet, a voice like waters, seven stars in His hand, a sword from His mouth and a face like the sun.

structure.label: The Commission (v. 17-20)
structure.body: John falls as if dead; Christ touches him, tells him not to fear, and declares Himself the First and Last, the Living One who was dead and holds the keys of death and Hades; John must write what he has seen, what is and what will be; the stars are the angels of the churches and the lampstands are the churches.

sections.heading: How to Read Revelation
paragraphs: The first verse tells us what kind of book this is. It is an ‘apocalypse’, an unveiling: “This is the Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show to his servants the things which must happen soon” (v. 1). It is also a ‘prophecy’: “Blessed is he who reads and those who hear the words of the prophecy” (v. 3). And it is a letter, addressed to seven real churches (v. 4). So Revelation must be read in three ways at once: as a picture-vision full of symbols, as God's word calling for a response, and as a message that first-century Christians could understand.

The word ‘made known’ in verse 1 is σημαίνω, ‘to show by signs’. Revelation tells us plainly that it speaks in symbols, and often explains them: the stars are angels, the lampstands are churches (v. 20). Most of its pictures come from the Old Testament — Daniel, Ezekiel, Zechariah, Isaiah, Exodus. A reader who knows those books will find Revelation far less strange.

Christians have read Revelation in four main ways. Some see most of it fulfilled in the first centuries (the preterist view); some see it as a map of church history (the historicist view); many see chapters 4–22 as mainly describing the events just before Christ's return (the futurist view); and others read it as a picture of the battle between Christ and evil in every age (the idealist view). Each has something true: Revelation spoke to its first readers, it describes realities that recur through history, and it looks forward to a real final coming of Christ. This study will take each vision in the way its own words suggest.

sections.heading: The Faithful Witness Who Loves Us
paragraphs: John's greeting is Trinitarian: grace and peace come “from God, who is and who was and who is to come; and from the seven Spirits who are before his throne; and from Jesus Christ” (vv. 4–5). Jesus is given three titles: “the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth” (v. 5). He was faithful to death, He rose first from death, and He now rules over every king — including Caesar. For believers facing a hostile empire, this is the place to start.

Then John bursts into praise: “To him who loves us, and washed us from our sins by his blood; and he made us to be a Kingdom, priests to his God and Father” (vv. 5–6). The order matters: He loves us (present), freed us (past), and made us a kingdom of priests (our new identity). The church is small and persecuted, but it is a royal priesthood — the true people of God.

And He is coming: “Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, including those who pierced him” (v. 7). John combines Daniel's son of man coming with the clouds and Zechariah's prophecy, “they will look to me whom they have pierced” (Zechariah 12:10). The One who was pierced will return in glory, and every eye will see Him.

sections.heading: One Like a Son of Man
paragraphs: John's vision of Jesus draws together Old Testament pictures of God Himself. The hair “white as white wool, like snow” (v. 14) is what Daniel saw of the Ancient of Days; the voice “like the voice of many waters” (v. 15) is how Ezekiel heard the glory of God. The title “I am the first and the last” (v. 17) is what God says in Isaiah. John is not seeing an angel or a great prophet; he is seeing the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.

Each detail of the vision will reappear in the letters to the churches. To Ephesus He is the one who holds the seven stars (2:1); to Smyrna the first and last, who was dead and came to life (2:8); to Pergamum the one with the sharp two-edged sword (2:12); to Thyatira the one with eyes like fire and feet like brass (2:18). The portrait of Christ is the medicine for each church's disease.

John's response is to fall as though dead (v. 17). The beloved disciple who once rested against Jesus' side cannot stand before His glory. But Jesus puts His right hand on him and says, “Don’t be afraid. I am the first and the last, and the Living one. I was dead, and behold, I am alive forever and ever. Amen. I have the keys of Death and of Hades” (vv. 17–18). That is the word every suffering believer needs: the One who holds the keys of death is the One who loves us.

sections.heading: Stars and Lampstands
paragraphs: Jesus explains two symbols: “The seven stars are the angels of the seven assemblies. The seven lamp stands are seven assemblies” (v. 20). The churches are lampstands, not lamps: they do not produce the light, they hold it up. Their purpose is to shine in a dark world. And Jesus walks among them — present, watching, caring, correcting.

Who are the ‘angels’ of the churches? The Greek word ἄγγελος means messenger as well as angel. Some think each church has a guardian angel; others think of the church's leaders or messengers; others think the ‘angel’ represents the church's heavenly identity. What is clear is that Christ holds them in His right hand. The church is never out of His grasp.

John is told to write “the things which you have seen, and the things which are, and the things which will happen hereafter” (v. 19). Many see here a simple outline of the whole book. Whether or not that is its purpose, it reminds us that Revelation speaks to the present as well as the future: what Jesus says to the churches is what ‘is’, and it is addressed to us.

ntConnection.heading: The Son of Man, Seen in Glory
paragraphs: Jesus called Himself the Son of Man and, at His trial, applied Daniel's vision to Himself: “you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of the sky” (Mark 14:62). At His ascension the angels said, “This Jesus, who was received up from you into the sky, will come back in the same way as you saw him going into the sky” (Acts 1:11). Revelation 1:7 picks up both.

John had seen this glory once before. On the mountain of transfiguration, “He was transfigured before them. His face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light” (Matthew 17:2), and the disciples “fell on their faces, and were very afraid” (Matthew 17:6). Then, as on Patmos, “Jesus came and touched them and said, ‘Get up, and don’t be afraid’” (Matthew 17:7).

John's Gospel also records the piercing: “However one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out” (John 19:34), and adds, “Again another Scripture says, ‘They will look on him whom they pierced’” (John 19:37). Hebrews says of Him that “he lives forever to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25) — the One John now sees robed as a priest, alive forever and ever.

lexicon.insight: Strong's: “disclosure.” ἀποκάλυψις is from ἀπό (away from) and καλύπτω (to cover): the removing of a cover, an unveiling. It gives the book its name in English (‘Apocalypse’). In popular speech ‘apocalypse’ means catastrophe; in the Bible it means disclosure — God drawing back the curtain to show what is really true about Jesus, about history and about the future. Everything in the book is ‘the Revelation of Jesus Christ’.

lexicon.strongs: G3144 (testimony μαρτυρία, martyría, G3141; testified μαρτυρέω, martyréō, G3140)
lexicon.insight: Strong's: “a witness (literally (judicially) or figuratively (genitive case)); by analogy, a "martyr".” Revelation is a book of witness: John testifies (v. 2), Jesus is the faithful witness (v. 5), John is on Patmos for the testimony of Jesus (v. 9), Antipas is ‘my faithful witness’ who was killed (2:13). By the end of the first century the word was moving from ‘one who testifies’ to ‘one who dies for the testimony’. Jesus is the first faithful martyr; His people follow Him.

Strong's: “the all-ruling, i.e. God (as absolute and universal sovereign).” παντοκράτωρ joins πᾶς (all) and κράτος (ruling power, from the power family). It appears nine times in Revelation and only once elsewhere in the New Testament (2 Corinthians 6:18). It translates the Old Testament ‘LORD of Armies’. In a world where Caesar claimed universal rule, Revelation insists that only one is the All-Ruler.

Strong's: “pressure (literally or figuratively).” θλῖψις is from θλίβω, to press, squeeze or crush, as grapes in a winepress. John shares it with his readers now (v. 9); Smyrna will face it (2:10); the multitude in white come ‘out of the great tribulation’ (7:14). In verse 9 θλῖψις, βασιλεία and ὑπομονή are bound together by one article: suffering, the kingdom and patient endurance are one package for the follower of Jesus.

Strong's: “a lamp-stand (literally or figuratively).” λυχνία, from λύχνος (lamp), is a stand that holds a lamp up so that its light can be seen. The tabernacle had one seven-branched lampstand; Zechariah saw a golden lampstand fed by olive trees, a picture of God's people shining by His Spirit. Revelation's seven lampstands are the churches (1:20), and two lampstands are the two witnesses (11:4). Jesus warns Ephesus that He can remove its lampstand (2:5): a church that stops shining loses its reason to exist.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: In this opening chapter the Holy Spirit wants to show you Jesus as He is now, and to change how you face your own trials.

items.title: Your Patmos Can Be Your Place of Vision
items.body: John was in exile “because of God’s Word and the testimony of Jesus Christ” (v. 9) — and there he saw the glory of Christ. The Spirit wants you to know that your hardest, loneliest place of faithfulness is not wasted. Worship there. Listen there. The voice may be just behind you.

items.title: Don't Be Afraid
items.body: The One whose eyes are like fire and whose face shines like the sun lays His right hand on John and says, “Don’t be afraid” (v. 17). The Spirit brings you that same word today. Whatever you fear — death, loss, failure, the future — Jesus holds the keys. He was dead and is alive forever.

items.title: He Walks Among the Lampstands
items.body: Jesus is not absent from His church. He walks among the lampstands and sees everything (v. 13). The Spirit wants you to take your church — its weakness, its faults, its faithfulness — and see it as Jesus sees it: precious, held in His right hand, and called to shine.

audit.title: The Vision Check
audit.body: When you picture Jesus, what do you see? A gentle teacher? A distant figure? Compare your picture with verses 13–18. What part of His glory have you lost sight of?

audit.title: The Fear Check
audit.body: What are you most afraid of? Bring it to the One who holds the keys of Death and of Hades (v. 18). What changes if He truly holds them?

audit.title: The Keeping Check
audit.body: The blessing of verse 3 is for those who ‘keep’ what is written. Are you reading the Bible for information or for obedience?

practices.title: Worship on the Lord's Day
practices.body: This Sunday, before you go to church, spend fifteen minutes alone reading Revelation 1:4–8 aloud as praise. Then, during the service, look around the room and remember: Jesus walks among the lampstands. Pray for your church as His.

practices.title: Write What You See
practices.body: Each day this week, read one part of the vision (vv. 12–18) and write down one thing it shows you about Jesus and one way it answers a fear or need in your life. At the end of the week, pray through your list with thanks.

prayerReflection: “Lord Jesus Christ, You are the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead and the ruler of the kings of the earth. You love me, and You freed me from my sins by Your blood. You have made me part of Your kingdom and a priest to Your God and Father. To You be the glory and the dominion forever and ever. I believe You are coming with the clouds, and every eye will see You. You are the Alpha and the Omega, the Almighty. When I am pressed and alone, let me hear Your voice behind me. Let me see You as You are — walking among Your churches, eyes like fire, face shining like the sun. I fall at Your feet. Lay Your right hand on me and tell me not to be afraid. You were dead, and You are alive forever and ever, and You hold the keys of death and Hades. Hold my church in Your right hand, and make us shine like a lampstand in the dark. Make me one who hears and keeps Your word. Amen.”

storyConnections.title: The Transfiguration
storyConnections.summary: Jesus took Peter, James and John up a high mountain, and was transfigured before them: “His face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light” (Matthew 17:2). A bright cloud covered them and the Father's voice spoke. The disciples fell on their faces in terror, “Jesus came and touched them and said, ‘Get up, and don’t be afraid’” (Matthew 17:7). Sixty years later on Patmos, John saw that same face shining like the sun, fell again, and felt again the touch of the same hand.

storyConnections.title: Daniel's Vision of the Son of Man
storyConnections.summary: In exile in Babylon, Daniel saw thrones set up, the Ancient of Days with hair ‘like pure wool’, and ‘one like a son of man’ coming with the clouds to receive an everlasting kingdom. Later by the river Tigris he saw a man whose face was like lightning and eyes like flaming torches; Daniel fell on his face, and a hand touched him with the words, ‘Don’t be afraid.’ John, in exile on Patmos, receives a vision shaped by Daniel's — and sees that the Son of Man is Jesus.

storyConnections.title: Zechariah's Golden Lampstand
storyConnections.summary: After the exile, the prophet Zechariah saw “a lamp stand all of gold, with its bowl on the top of it” (Zechariah 4:2), fed by two olive trees. The message was for the small, weak community rebuilding the temple: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit” (Zechariah 4:6). Revelation's lampstands carry the same message to small, weak churches in a mighty empire: they shine not by their own power but by the Spirit of the One who walks among them.
